title: How Mac Got Fat

jokes.text: Mac opens his confession with 'I'm fat.' — a long pause after the elaborate confessional setup
jokes.setup: The formal confessional ritual is established; priest asks for the confession with solemnity
jokes.punchline: After a long beat (00:14 to 00:40 gap suggests a pause), Mac's entire confession is simply 'I'm fat' — the most mundane possible self-revelation in the most sacred possible context
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — three words do enormous work. The confessional framing implies a deep moral failing; 'I'm fat' is simultaneously too trivial for confession and genuinely the thesis of the episode. The gap (timestamp jumps from 00:14 to 00:40) implies a comedic beat of silence before Mac elaborates. Perfect character integration: Mac's combination of religious sincerity and total lack of self-awareness makes this land exactly right. Earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I'm fat.

jokes.text: Mac shouts 'O great and angry God, I command thee to smite my friends!' inside a confessional booth
jokes.setup: Mac is in confession — a setting of humble repentance and private introspection
jokes.punchline: He erupts into a commanding, theatrical invocation demanding God smite his friends, treating confession like a customer complaint line to God
jokes.explanation: Mac's faux-pious yet entitled religious worldview is the core of his character, and this moment crystallizes it. He genuinely believes he can command God and use confession as an escalation pathway. The theatrical phrasing ('thee,' 'smite') contrasted with his petty grievance is a sharp juxtaposition. Highly quotable for Sunny fans.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, great and angry God, I command thee to smite my friends!

jokes.text: Mac: 'So, really, I'd like to confess on them, because they're sinners and pricks.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been building a case that his friends caused his sin
jokes.punchline: He announces he wants to confess ON BEHALF of his friends — fundamentally misunderstanding the sacrament — and caps it with 'pricks,' the vulgarity shattering the sacred register
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'confess on them' is a beautiful malapropism/concept error — Mac treating confession like snitching to God. The word 'pricks' in a confessional is a tonal collision that lands well. Character-specific: only Mac's specific brand of Catholic entitlement makes this work.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: So, really, I'd like to confess on them, because they're sinners and pricks.

jokes.text: Mac tells the priest he needs 'the context' and launches into an elaborate flashback story about bar success when asked to stay on himself.
jokes.setup: The priest gently explains that Mac is misusing confession.
jokes.punchline: Mac acknowledges this, apologizes, and then immediately proceeds to do exactly the same thing — derailing into a lengthy third-person story about his friends.
jokes.explanation: This is structural/framing comedy — the whole episode is built on this joke. The setup works as a premise-establisher. The humor comes from Mac's total inability to follow the most basic instruction while believing he's being cooperative. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Son, I don't think you understand the purpose of confession.

jokes.text: Mac's 'we may have tipped' speech — each gang member claims personal credit for the bar's success (cleanliness, comedy, appearance)
jokes.setup: The gang is mystified by their bar's sudden popularity; Mac references 'The Tipping Point'
jokes.punchline: Each character immediately assigns 100% of the credit to their own specific vanity — Charlie's 'clean bar,' Dee's 'one-liners,' Dennis's hair and appearance — none remotely self-aware
jokes.explanation: A round-robin of narcissism where each character's self-aggrandizement perfectly reflects their established delusions. Charlie's domestic pride, Dee's comedic delusion, Dennis's physical vanity — all perfectly calibrated. The joke is that they're ALL doing it simultaneously and each is fully convinced. Strong ensemble character work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: What the shit is going on around here?

jokes.text: Dee credits the bar's success to herself being 'the cute, funny waitress' with 'one-liners and hilarious jabs'
jokes.setup: Everyone is claiming individual credit for the bar's success
jokes.punchline: Dee calls herself 'cute' and 'funny' — the audience knows she is neither, and her comedy is a recurring failure
jokes.explanation: Dee's delusion about her comedy talent is a series-long running gag that pays off harder later in the episode. Here it's setup. The 'cute' self-description is funny given the show's established running mockery of Dee's appearance. Good but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's like that book The Tipping Point.

jokes.text: Mac's summary of the gang's flaws: 'No matter how psychotically vain... or needy and pathetic or, I mean, just plain sad.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to frame their collective behavior as a positive thing that caused success
jokes.punchline: His list of 'strengths' slides into increasingly brutal self-owns — 'psychotically vain,' 'needy and pathetic,' 'just plain sad' — while remaining motivational in tone
jokes.explanation: The escalating self-diagnosis while maintaining a pep-talk cadence is a solid ironic structure. The gang nods along while being described as pathetic, which is the real joke. Competent writing, not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm like the cute, funny waitress who has all these one-liners and hilarious jabs I throw at the customers

jokes.text: Frank wakes Charlie to pitch: 'We take the M-80's that I have... and we stick 'em in some lamb. And pa-chow! We blow it up!'
jokes.setup: Mac has explicitly told everyone to get a good night's sleep; Frank wakes Charlie to share a 'great idea'
jokes.punchline: Frank's 'great idea' is to detonate M-80 fireworks inside a lamb — a meat bomb — presented with complete enthusiasm as if this is a coherent plan
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank — genuinely terrible idea delivered with total conviction. The specificity (lamb, M-80s, 'pa-chow') makes it funnier than a vague 'blow something up' joke. The sound effect 'pa-chow' is a nice touch of childlike enthusiasm. Well-integrated into Frank's character as someone who operates outside normal logic.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No matter how psychotically vain... or needy and pathetic or, I mean, just plain sad.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'What are you looking to do? Flash-cook a... a gyro sandwich?' / Frank: 'Yeah. That's a good idea.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to understand Frank's meat bomb plan by translating it into real-world terms
jokes.punchline: Charlie's rhetorical/dismissive question ('flash-cook a gyro?') is immediately adopted by Frank as a legitimately great idea — the absurdity accepted without irony
jokes.explanation: The structure here is tight: Charlie's attempt to dismiss via reductio ad absurdum backfires because Frank accepts the absurd premise enthusiastically. 'Cook the meat immediately' as elaboration is perfect. The joke has two beats and both land. Strong economy — the exchange is four lines total and completely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What are you looking to do? Like, flash-cook a-a gyro sandwich?

jokes.text: Charlie: 'What you're talking about is just a meat bomb. That's a waste of a good lamb.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to shut down Frank's lamb-explosion plan
jokes.punchline: His objection to the meat bomb is not safety, not legality, not sanity — it's that it wastes good lamb. This is his actual moral concern.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie logic. His objection is entirely practical from within the internal universe where exploding lamb might otherwise be acceptable — the only issue is meat waste. The phrase 'a good lamb' is specific enough to be very funny. Strong economy and excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: A meat bomb!

jokes.text: Charlie retreats to 'the crevice' — Frank desperately pleads 'Don't go in the crevice, Charlie'
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie's argument escalates; Charlie threatens to retreat
jokes.punchline: Charlie retreats to 'the crevice' — a location treated as a real, established escape hatch in their shared living space, apparently known well enough that Frank specifically names it and dreads it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes because it's entirely unexplained. 'The crevice' is never defined, which makes it funnier — clearly a known location, clearly unpleasant enough that Frank doesn't want Charlie to go there, and clearly Charlie uses it as leverage. The specificity of the name, Frank's panic, and the total absence of explanation all work together. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value as viewers try to piece together what the crevice is.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm going to the crevice!

jokes.text: Mac calling to 'go rage' while Charlie announces from the crevice: 'I don't care. I'm in the crevice.'
jokes.setup: Mac calls to invite Charlie out; Frank relays the message
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response from inside the crevice — a dignified, utterly committed 'I don't care. I'm in the crevice.' — delivered as though it's a perfectly normal situation
jokes.explanation: The callback to the crevice lands even harder because Charlie doubles down on its reality. His flat, committed delivery ('I'm in the crevice') treats this as a completely valid reason to decline social plans. The economy is superb — six words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Charlie, don't go in the crevice.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Dennis always tells me, never let someone's resistance stop you from getting what you want.' — used to justify ignoring the priest's perfectly reasonable redirection
jokes.setup: The priest tries to steer Mac toward actual confession
jokes.punchline: Mac quotes Dennis's deeply predatory life philosophy as wisdom justifying his ignoring the priest — revealing both Mac's uncritical admiration for Dennis and Dennis's sociopathy through a single quote
jokes.explanation: This is efficient double-character comedy — it simultaneously reveals Mac's total deference to Dennis and Dennis's deeply concerning worldview (which reads as sexual-predator logic applied universally). Using it in a confessional context is a sharp ironic touch. The joke does a lot of work in one sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Kids these days, they have so many more choices than we had when we were little. Am I right?

jokes.text: Dee trying to tell a joke to bar customers who keep interrupting her to order drinks
jokes.setup: Dee fancies herself a comedian; she's supposed to be waitressing
jokes.punchline: She keeps attempting to deliver a joke about kids and choices while customers interrupt for actual drinks; she prioritizes the joke over her job, getting progressively agitated
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee cringe — her delusion about her comedic talent vs. the reality of customers who just want drinks. The extended nature of it (multiple interruptions) escalates nicely. The joke she keeps trying to tell is intentionally terrible ('kids these days have so many more choices'), which layers the comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, they're not landing because I'm not getting to the punch line

jokes.text: Dee's joke attempt: 'Kids these days, they have so many more choices than we had when we were little. Am I right?' — the actual joke content is revealed to be completely banal
jokes.setup: Dee insists her joke would be funny if she could just get to the punchline
jokes.punchline: The setup we hear is profoundly unfunny — a hacky, nothing observational premise — making her conviction that it's brilliant the actual joke
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke about a bad joke is well-executed. Dee's joke is exactly the kind of lazy, premise-only observational humor that wouldn't survive a good comedy room. Her total conviction makes it funnier. The 'Do you want to watch Kung Fu Panda on Blu-ray' detail implies the punchline involves that, which makes it even worse.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I drank three bottles of champagne and hung out with a stray dog all night under a bridge

jokes.text: Dee escalates: 'You're not getting your margarita' as punishment for the customer interrupting her joke.
jokes.setup: Customer says they don't want to hear Dee's joke, they just want their margarita.
jokes.punchline: Dee weaponizes drink service as revenge for the audience refusing to listen to her comedy — a stunning inversion of the service relationship.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from annoying comedian to petty authoritarian bartender is a good beat. Dee treating her comedy as more important than customer service reveals her narcissism cleanly. The delivery of 'You're not getting your margarita. Thanks.' is very Dee.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: your jokes never land, all right? So please don't concentrate on your comedy anymore, 'cause it's terrible

jokes.text: Charlie arrives for work: 'I drank three bottles of champagne and hung out with a stray dog all night under a bridge. It was sweet.'
jokes.setup: Mac asks where Charlie has been after he dramatically oversleeps
jokes.punchline: The explanation is a portrait of Charlie's lifestyle — three bottles of champagne, stray dog, under a bridge — delivered with genuine warmth and satisfaction ('It was sweet')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity is perfect — not just 'drinking,' not just 'outside,' but three bottles of champagne (incongruous luxury) + stray dog (perfect Charlie companion) + under a bridge (his natural habitat) + 'It was sweet' (his genuine contentment with this life). Pure Charlie Kelly in one sentence. Highly quotable. The deadpan delivery of 'It was sweet' as a sincere endorsement is the killer beat.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm bashing it.

jokes.text: Dee: 'Can I please get, like, 20 margaritas so this bitch will listen to my kid joke?'
jokes.setup: Dee has been fighting with a customer about her joke; she turns to Charlie for help
jokes.punchline: Her request to Charlie is to make 20 margaritas as a bribe/gesture to earn the right to tell one joke — a wildly disproportionate solution — and she calls the customer 'this bitch' casually
jokes.explanation: Funny in context — the '20 margaritas' escalation is good, and 'this bitch' is a casually terrible thing to say about a customer. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I saw a couple gray hairs, and I was, like, 'I'll eradicate those,' and then...

jokes.text: Dennis has been in the bathroom for an hour; when confronted: 'I'm bashing it. I'm bashing it!'
jokes.setup: The gang discovers Dennis has been in the bathroom for an hour during peak bar service
jokes.punchline: 'I'm bashing it' — context reveals he's doing something to his appearance (later revealed as dyeing gray hairs), but the phrase sounds alarming out of context and his panic at being found is funny
jokes.explanation: Good buildup with the hour-long bathroom mystery. 'Bashing it' is appropriately cryptic. The misdirection (sounds bad, turns out to be narcissistic grooming) is a reasonable structure. Competent but doesn't quite reach exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You look like Superman.

jokes.text: Dennis exits the bathroom having dyed his hair jet black to cover gray — with black paint — and is told 'You look like Superman'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been grooming in the bathroom, motivated by his terror of losing physical perfection
jokes.punchline: He has apparently applied black hair dye so heavily (or literally used paint) that he looks exactly like Superman — a visual gag where Dennis's narcissism has produced the opposite of a natural result
jokes.explanation: Strong visual gag — the Superman comparison is specific enough to be funny (not just 'you look like a cartoon character'). Dennis's immediate positive reception ('Oh, cool. Yeah, right on. Well, he was the original, right?') before realizing the insult is classic Dennis: vanity before logic. The beats that follow ('You'd be, Shit, maybe that's Superman') escalate nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, shit. Maybe that's Superman.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'It wouldn't be that obvious if you didn't know me. You'd be, Shit. Maybe that's Superman.'
jokes.setup: Mac and others point out that his dyed hair makes him look obviously like Superman
jokes.punchline: Dennis genuinely believes that a stranger might mistake him for Superman, which requires both mistaking him for a fictional character AND for a physically superior alien superhero
jokes.explanation: Dennis's specific, earnest logic — 'if you didn't know me' as the key variable, as though the problem is familiarity rather than the fact that Superman is fictional — reveals his solipsism perfectly. The phrasing 'Shit. Maybe that's Superman' as an imagined passerby's internal monologue is very specific and very funny. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I got some donuts and some M&Ms and some, uh, chips. I could pass them through if you want some.

jokes.text: Mac: 'We can't be Superman!' — delivered as an earnest motivational rallying cry against hubris
jokes.setup: The gang is unraveling; Mac is trying to give a coherent pep talk
jokes.punchline: Mac's most urgent piece of advice in this crisis is 'We can't be Superman' — which only makes sense if the alternative being seriously considered was 'being Superman'
jokes.explanation: A good callback beat — it re-grounds the Superman riff and reveals that Mac's version of a reality check is still operating at an absurd level. Functional, gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Are you eating in there?

jokes.text: Mac's narration shifts: Charlie, in a falsetto impression, mocks Mac's speech — 'Back to work. Back to work, everybody. I'm Charlie, and I'm in charge all of a sudden.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been narrating with self-importance about how he tried to hold the team together
jokes.punchline: Charlie (in Mac's retelling) mocks Mac's leadership pretensions with a spot-on impression — revealing that Mac's 'in charge' moment was not received as intended
jokes.explanation: Good meta-narrative joke — the fact that Mac is NARRATING this mockery of himself without realizing what it means is funny. Charlie's impression (even as rendered by Mac) deflates Mac's self-appointed leadership. Character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Hey, that's good. You want to do that to people?

jokes.text: Mac is interrupted mid-narration by the priest eating — the priest has doughnuts, M&Ms, and chips in the confessional, offers to pass some through
jokes.setup: Mac is in the middle of a dramatic narration in a confessional
jokes.punchline: The priest is snacking — not on a small thing but doughnuts, M&Ms, AND chips — and casually offers to share through the confessional screen, completely undercutting the sanctity of the setting
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly good joke — the priest snacking is funny, but 'I could pass them through if you want some' is what elevates it. The specificity of three different snacks establishes he's really dug in, and his casual offer implies this is totally normal to him. The confessional screen as a snack-sharing window is an absurd image. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank, you've just created a four-way intersection. If anything, you've made this intersection safer.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I'm done. Done.' — immediately after being caught eating in the confessional, he insists he's finished and returns to narrating.
jokes.setup: Priest tells Mac to put the food away or leave.
jokes.punchline: Mac defensively insists he's done eating, then immediately pivots back to his story — suggesting this was a brief but serious crisis that is now resolved.
jokes.explanation: A functional button on the snacking gag. Not exceptional on its own but serves the rhythm of the frame narrative.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dee is guilty of sloth, and she's pro-abortion.

jokes.text: Frank has installed extra stop signs at an intersection — four stop signs — and presents this as a devious plan
jokes.setup: Frank spent all night working on a plan to show Charlie
jokes.punchline: The plan is four stop signs at an intersection. When Charlie points out he's just made it a four-way stop (safer), Frank says 'No shit' — a beat of genuine surprise and disappointment
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Frank's plan — adding stop signs to an intersection — is exactly the right level of stupid: it sounds like it could be mischievous (blocking traffic, causing chaos) but is in fact just standard traffic infrastructure. Charlie's explanation ('you've just created a four-way intersection — if anything, you've made this safer') and Frank's flat 'No shit' of genuine realization is the perfect button. Frank's reaction — taking it in, processing it — is what makes it land. Excellent structure, perfect character work, memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I don't want to go to any poor places, you know. Successful guy like myself, I'll have a target on my back.

jokes.text: Frank hits Charlie with a stick and insists 'This is the plan. This is the one we should have done.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Charlie's stop sign conversation has ended in failure
jokes.punchline: Frank's new 'plan' is apparently just hitting Charlie with a stick, which he presents with the same entrepreneurial confidence as the meat bomb and stop signs
jokes.explanation: Physical gag with a decent callback structure — Frank applies the same confidence to 'hit Charlie with stick' as to his actual plans. The joke is that there's no plan, but Frank's enthusiasm for it is perfect. Competent, slightly underdeveloped.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You're just going to sail around the United States is what it looks like.

jokes.text: Mac's narration: 'And Charlie was, like, I'm gonna jam that stick up your ass! And then Frank was, like, Come here, you little bitch!' — priest interrupts: 'You don't need to repeat all of the obscene language.'
jokes.setup: Mac is narrating the Frank/Charlie altercation with obvious enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Mac is enthusiastically performing all the profanity of the fight for the priest; the priest gently corrects him; Mac responds: 'I got lost in the moment because I'm a natural storyteller'
jokes.explanation: Mac's self-description as 'a natural storyteller' is a strong character beat — his self-flattery is consistent with his overall delusion. The priest interruption is a good structural device. The profanity relay in a confessional has inherent comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I got a chemical peel.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Lazy's a sin, right?' / Priest: 'Uh, you mean sloth?' / Mac: 'Yeah, yeah. Dee is guilty of sloth. And she's pro-abortion.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to frame Dee's behavior as sinful in the confessional context
jokes.punchline: He correctly identifies sloth, then immediately adds 'and she's pro-abortion' as an equivalent moral crime, delivered with the same matter-of-fact listing tone as the theological sin
jokes.explanation: Excellent compression — three things happen simultaneously: (1) Mac's religious piety is confirmed, (2) his political views are revealed with no preamble, (3) the conflation of theological sin with political position is a character-specific logical move only Mac would make. The absolute flat delivery — 'and she's pro-abortion' — as a postscript to sloth is what makes it sing. Perfect economy. High quotability for Sunny fans.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was just trying to live up to all of your expectations of me. Physical perfection.

jokes.text: Mac's map of the world eliminating all sailing destinations: Africa (poor), unnamed cold regions (too cold), unnamed hot regions (too violent, too hot, too angry) — leaving only a loop around the continental US
jokes.setup: Mac is planning his success-era sailing itinerary
jokes.punchline: His geographic reasoning eliminates most of the world for varying degrees of prejudice and inconvenience, with Dee's dry one-word responses affirming each exclusion, until his world sailing trip is revealed to be a coastal US loop
jokes.explanation: Good escalating joke — each exclusion gets more revealing about Mac's worldview. The rhythm of Dee's affirmations ('Yeah,' 'Right,' 'Oh, the whole thing') as a Greek chorus is effective. The payoff (just the US) is well-structured. Slightly weakened by being a list joke without a truly surprising final item.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: it looks like you're wearing a mask of yourself over your face. Not a good one.

jokes.text: Mac also eliminates part of the United States from his sailing map: 'And I don't know what happens out here.'
jokes.setup: Mac has already narrowed his sailing to just the US
jokes.punchline: He further eliminates an unspecified region of his own country as a no-go zone
jokes.explanation: Good button on the sailing map joke. His fear of an unidentified part of his own country after dismissing most of the world on specific grounds is a funny escalation. 'I don't know what happens out here' is a good vague fear line.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: When I leave the gym, and I have a full pump...

jokes.text: Dennis found hiding under the covers — revealed to have gotten a chemical peel — 'You look like a monster, dude.'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee try to get Dennis's input on the avatar plan; he's hiding under covers
jokes.punchline: He emerges with a chemical peel face — raw, red, possibly peeling — described as 'wearing a mask of yourself over your face, not a good one'
jokes.explanation: Dennis's escalating body horror in service of physical perfection is consistent character work. The description 'wearing a mask of yourself over your face' is a genuinely unsettling and funny image. The visual gag carries most of the weight here.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Father, when Peter did the statue of David, he wasn't just hammering at pebbles. First, he ordered the Jews to bring him a massive slab of marble.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Right now it looks like you're wearing a mask of yourself over your face. Not a good one.' / Dennis: 'Not a nice mask of myself? Do you guys think that a normal mask of me would look good? And if there was, would you guys wear it?'
jokes.setup: Mac tells Dennis his chemical peel looks like a bad mask of himself
jokes.punchline: Dennis pivots from horror at the insult to earnest inquiry: would a GOOD mask of him look good? Would they wear it? — his narcissism overrides the insult and he moves straight to merchandising his own face
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. Dennis's narcissism is so perfectly calibrated: he absorbs a devastating insult, then immediately redirects to whether a hypothetical GOOD mask of him would be appealing, and would they wear it. This is a character-specific joke that could only come from Dennis — his solipsism so complete that the concept of his own face as a wearable product is a natural next thought. 'Would you guys wear it?' is the killer line. Highly quotable, strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I dip it in bleach, then it's clean!

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I'm going to be alone.'
jokes.setup: Dennis's mask question is met with confusion and alarm
jokes.punchline: His conclusion — delivered flatly, with apparent genuine insight — is 'I'm going to be alone.' Not that his face looks bad, not that his plan was wrong, but a moment of existential clarity about his ultimate fate, delivered in the same register as a weather observation
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. Dennis pivots from 'would you wear a mask of my face' to 'I'm going to be alone' — a sudden depth charge of dark self-awareness that cuts through the narcissism. It works as a joke (absurd non-sequitur pivot) AND as genuine character revelation. The flatness is crucial — he's not fishing for comfort, he's just filing a report on his own future. Perfect economy (10/10), strong character integration. This is Sunny at its best: dark, funny, and sad simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Because I'm dipping them in bleach so that I can clean them faster. I don't have time to wash every single glass. I dip it in bleach, then it's clean!

jokes.text: Mac and Dee interview job candidates: Mac asks the applicant to do dumbbell curls 'but don't do it in a normal way' — 'This is for a bartending job, right?'
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are interviewing potential 'avatar' employees
jokes.punchline: The interview involves weightlifting, explicitly for a bartending position, and Mac's instruction to do it 'in a normal way' inverted is the tell that this has nothing to do with bartending
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of a strength-based bartending interview is a solid premise. The applicant's completely reasonable question ('This is for a bartending job, right?') grounds it. Competent comedy that sets up stronger payoffs.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Then get out of my bar! Get out of my bar!

jokes.text: Dee: 'He looks nothing like you.' Mac: 'Well, no. Since we've been working, I've been neglecting my fitness regimen.' / Dee: 'You never, ever once in your life have looked like that.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to fast-track the muscular applicant as his avatar because 'he understands'
jokes.punchline: Mac claims the difference between him and the avatar is recent gym neglect; Dee categorically demolishes this by clarifying Mac has NEVER looked like that, not recently
jokes.explanation: Dee's flat correction — 'you never, ever once in your life have looked like that' — is the perfect puncture of Mac's delusion. The specificity of 'never, ever once in your life' is funnier than 'you've never looked like that.' Good straight-man/delusional-man structure.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm running at of ten of excellence, and I'm used to being at whatever number.

jokes.text: Mac's narration: 'Father, when Peter did the statue of David, he wasn't just hammering at pebbles. First, he ordered the Jews to bring him a massive slab of marble.'
jokes.setup: Priest asks if Mac went to the gym to bulk up for the avatar
jokes.punchline: Mac's explanation for why he ate massive amounts of food instead of going to the gym invokes Michelangelo (attributed to 'Peter'), misidentifies the artist, misattributes the material sourcing to 'the Jews,' and uses the entire thing as a logical justification for eating
jokes.explanation: Excellent multi-layered joke. Mac's false wisdom here hits several notes simultaneously: (1) Wrong artist ('Peter' instead of Michelangelo), (2) The actual point of the metaphor is 'you need raw material before you sculpt' applied to gaining weight, (3) The aside about 'ordering the Jews' is a casually offensive historical invention, (4) The logic, while absurd, is internally coherent in Mac's universe. The confidence with which false knowledge is delivered is a Mac specialty. Highly quotable.

dialogue.line: ♪ Big, fat, big, fat Big, fat titties Big, fat ass. ♪

jokes.text: Charlie argues with a customer about drink orders: 'Well, with an attitude like that, you can wait another half an hour, buddy.'
jokes.setup: A customer who has been waiting 30 minutes for a Jack and Coke complains
jokes.punchline: Charlie's customer service response is to threaten additional wait time as punishment for the complaint — a bartender using extended service delay as a disciplinary tool
jokes.explanation: Classic Paddy's customer service. The inversion (complaint = more punishment) is a reliable structure. Slightly predictable but well-delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: But you have candy coming out of your pocket.

jokes.text: Charlie: 'This drink tastes like bleach.' / Charlie: 'Because I'm dipping them in bleach so that I can clean them faster. I dip it in bleach! Then it's clean!'
jokes.setup: A customer complains their drink tastes like bleach
jokes.punchline: Charlie confirms the bleach contamination and explains his dishwashing shortcut — dipping glasses in bleach instead of washing them — with the confidence of someone who has discovered a great efficiency hack
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The bleach-glass joke works on multiple levels: Charlie's completely non-defensive, matter-of-fact explanation reveals he sees no problem whatsoever with serving bleach-tainted drinks. 'I dip it in bleach! Then it's clean!' delivered as genuine problem-solving pride is perfect character work. The exclamation mark delivery ('Then it's clean!') as though he's cracked a code is what elevates this from a gross joke to a great character joke. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: if I smite your friends and absolve you, will you leave?

jokes.text: Customer: 'I'm not drinking bleach.' / Charlie: 'Then get out of my bar! Get out of my bar! I don't want to see you!'
jokes.setup: Customer refuses to drink the bleach-tainted glass
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds to the customer's entirely reasonable refusal with fury and eviction — he takes the customer's objection to being poisoned as a personal affront
jokes.explanation: Good escalation from the bleach revelation — Charlie's indignation at the customer's refusal to be poisoned maintains the inverted logic. 'Get out of my bar' as a response to 'I'm not drinking bleach' is the right amount of absurd. The callback structure ('become friends on your walk home') adds a nice button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: When does the spell kick in? When is God going to shed some of this weight for me?

jokes.text: Charlie insults two strangers who don't know each other: 'Okay, well, become friends on your walk home! Get out!'
jokes.setup: Charlie throws out a customer; a second customer says he doesn't even know the first one
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response — 'Become friends on your walk home!' — is both an insult and an oddly optimistic suggestion, as if he's doing them a favor by evicting them together
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — 'become friends on your walk home' is a great line. It has the cadence of a parting gift from Charlie, as though he's being genuinely helpful while evicting them. The optimism embedded in an eviction line is unexpected and funny. Strong economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: glory unto you, ghost man in the sky, that created us all and pre-determines everything.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I've created a level of success for myself that I just don't know if I can live up to anymore... I'm running at a 10 of excellence, and I'm used to being at whatever number.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is spiraling while failing at bartending with a chemical-peel face
jokes.punchline: His self-description of excellence — 'running at a 10' — immediately undermined by 'I'm used to being at whatever number,' suggesting he doesn't actually know or care what his baseline was, only that 10 is the new standard
jokes.explanation: 'At whatever number' as a self-assessment is a funny reveal — Dennis genuinely didn't track his previous performance level, only that 10 is now where he is. Good character beat, slightly less punchy than the best Dennis moments.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Hey, being on the tipping point is about working hard and caring about that work and really giving it your all. Let's get high in the back office.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just delivered what sounds like a genuine motivational speech about work ethic
jokes.punchline: The punchline arrives with no pause — 'Let's get high in the back office' — immediately detonating everything he just said
jokes.explanation: Perfect misdirection with excellent economy. The structure is a textbook setup/punchline — genuine-sounding speech about hard work immediately followed by 'Let's get high in the back office' with no transition. The lack of pause is crucial: Dennis doesn't even acknowledge the contradiction. The rhythm of the sentence ('caring about that work and really giving it your all. Let's get high.') is excellent joke writing. High quotability.

jokes.text: Frank wants Dee to hold a pigeon while he stuffs an M-80 under its wing and blows up the flock for 'a lot of tasty meat'
jokes.setup: The bar has emptied; Frank and Dee are standing around
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to the downtime is to detonate pigeons for food — a callback to his M-80 obsession from the meat bomb plan, now applied to wildlife — presented with complete practicality ('we got a lot of tasty meat')
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the M-80 theme — Frank's obsession with explosive cooking has migrated from lamb to pigeons. 'Tasty meat' as the goal of pigeon detonation is very Frank. Dee's objection ('terrible publicity for a young comedienne') is a great character response — her concern is her comedy career, not the animal cruelty.

jokes.text: Dee's objection to the pigeon bomb: 'That would be terrible publicity for a young comedienne.'
jokes.setup: Frank asks Dee to help him detonate a pigeon with an M-80
jokes.punchline: Dee's refusal is not 'that's animal cruelty' but 'that would be terrible publicity for a young comedienne' — her only concern is her comedy career branding
jokes.explanation: One of Dee's best lines. The phrase 'a young comedienne' applied to Dee is already funny (she is not young, she is not successful, she is barely a comedienne), but her reframing of pigeon bombing as a PR issue rather than a moral one is perfect Dee logic. Only Dee would think this way. Tight, character-specific, quotable.

jokes.text: Mac narrates what he imagines the stoned gang said: including Dee announcing she's 'pro-abortion' and 'going straight to hell,' and Frank saying 'I got fat. I'm much fatter than Mac! Big, fat titties. Big, fat ass. I like to kill babies. Unborn babies.'
jokes.setup: Mac is narrating what happened in the back office when the gang got high.
jokes.punchline: The 'imagined' conversation is an escalating absurdist sequence of non-sequiturs that reveals Mac's assumptions about his friends' inner lives — including Frank's body-image commentary and Dee's casual hell-bound admission.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Mac is fabricating this entire scene — 'I'm not exactly sure how that conversation went, but I imagine it was along those lines' — is a great meta-frame joke. The escalation from pro-abortion to 'I like to kill babies. Unborn babies.' captures Frank's feral bluntness. Mac's imagination of Dee as enthusiastically destined for hell is good character comedy.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I'm not exactly sure how that conversation went, but I imagine it was along those lines.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just narrated an elaborate drug-session conversation he wasn't present for
jokes.punchline: He casually admits he made the whole thing up, delivered with no embarrassment — having just confessed a completely fabricated account to a priest in the context of a sacrament
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the previous joke — the casual admission that the entire preceding narration was fabricated, delivered mid-confession to a priest, with zero self-awareness about the problem this creates. The understatement ('I imagine it was along those lines') as a confession qualifier is very funny. Great economy.

jokes.text: Frank wants to 'boil the blood' before replacing his blood with hospital blood bags to become 'more virile'
jokes.setup: Six weeks later; Frank, Charlie, and Dennis are discussing a plan
jokes.punchline: The plan is to transfuse Frank with bags of blood found behind a hospital ('not replace — ADD to it, to make me more virile'), and Frank's precaution is to boil the blood first
jokes.explanation: Classic Frank medical horror. The escalating specificity — found behind a hospital, boiling as a safety measure, additive rather than replacement transfusion for virility — is very Frank. Dennis's objection ('It doesn't matter if you boil it, Charlie') is the straight-man beat that grounds the absurdity. 'So you're just gonna be bursting at the seams with blood?' is a wonderfully gross image.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'So you're just gonna be bursting at the seams with blood?'
jokes.setup: Frank explains he wants to ADD blood rather than replace it
jokes.punchline: Dennis's visualisation of the logical endpoint — 'bursting at the seams with blood' — delivered with mild, clinical concern as though this is a minor logistical issue rather than a terrifying image
jokes.explanation: Good economy — 'bursting at the seams with blood' is a viscerally funny phrase. Dennis's flat delivery of a grotesque concept as a practical concern is effective. The image itself carries the joke.

jokes.text: Mac arrives announcing 'I did it. I'm 200 pounds. I'm as big as my avatar.' — having genuinely gained significant weight eating for six weeks
jokes.setup: Mac was supposed to be bulking up to match his muscular job applicant avatar
jokes.punchline: Mac has achieved 200 pounds — not muscle but simple weight gain from eating — beaming with accomplishment while the gang stares at a fat Mac
jokes.explanation: The payoff the entire episode has been building toward. Mac's achievement — 200 pounds of food-weight, not muscle — is a perfect character punchline. His pride is completely genuine and completely misplaced. The visual (a noticeably fatter Mac announcing this with triumph) is the essential component. Strong structure as an episode-long payoff.

jokes.text: Gang reveals the avatar plan was abandoned 'a million plans ago' — Mac had no idea and was eating in service of a dead plan
jokes.setup: Mac arrives triumphant at 200 pounds, ready to begin the avatar plan
jokes.punchline: The gang reveals the plan was dropped long ago; Mac has been gaining weight for nothing; the gang has 'been engaged in many other plans and schemes since then'
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the episode. Everything has been building to this: Mac gained 40+ pounds in service of a plan that was already dead. The gang's bafflement ('Why do you think we've been calling you fat this entire time?') and Mac's dawning horror is a great comedic beat. 'A million plans ago' as the gang's casual memory of their own schemes perfectly captures the show's ethos. Well-earned, not cheap.

jokes.text: Mac: 'D-Don't make fun of me, okay? I'm busting my ass out there trying to do the avatar plan.' / Gang laughs / Mac: 'But you have candy coming out of your pocket!'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to defend himself emotionally against the gang's mockery
jokes.punchline: While delivering a sincere plea for respect, candy is literally falling out of Mac's pocket — his bulk-eating addiction is physically manifesting mid-speech
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best visual gags. The candy-falling-from-pocket is a perfect physical comedy beat that arrives at exactly the right moment — during Mac's most earnest self-defense. 'You have candy coming out of your pocket!' interrupting his dignity is excellent comic timing. The image (fat Mac, candy streaming from pocket, trying to be taken seriously) is very funny and character-perfect. Strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Mac: 'I was hungry! I was hungry! Don't laugh at me!'
jokes.setup: Gang laughs at the candy falling from his pocket
jokes.punchline: Mac's dignified defense collapses into 'I was hungry!' — repeated, emphatic, as if hunger justifies everything — while continuing to demand they stop laughing
jokes.explanation: Good escalation beat — Mac's defensiveness is both funny and sad. The double 'I was hungry!' has a good rhythm. Part of a larger comedic sequence that lands well together.

jokes.text: Mac attempts to rip his shirt off in anger but can't do it — presumably because his new body mass makes it too tight or he lacks the core strength
jokes.setup: Mac is furious and trying to storm off dramatically
jokes.punchline: He attempts the classic dramatic shirt rip but his fat body either prevents it or makes it comedically difficult — the Gang mocks him for it
jokes.explanation: Inferred from 'Is he trying to rip his shirt off? He can't do it!' — a visual gag that lands because Mac's body-image delusion collides with the reality of his new weight. The shirt-rip is a classic machismo gesture, and its failure is a perfect cap to the scene. Strong character integration — Mac still thinks he's the ripped version of himself.

jokes.text: Mac: 'You guys are going to hell! Okay? You guys are going to hell!'
jokes.setup: Mac's emotional breakdown peaks as he fails to rip his shirt
jokes.punchline: His parting shot is a sincere theological condemnation — 'you guys are going to hell' — delivered as his ultimate weapon/insult, which only matters if you share Mac's Catholic worldview (which none of them do)
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac — when all else fails, invoke damnation. It's his most powerful rhetorical weapon and completely toothless against this gang. The character integration is strong. Slightly less punchy than the candy/shirt rip beats that precede it.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Father, my friends totally boned me.' — describing being betrayed as being 'boned'
jokes.setup: Mac concludes his confession story
jokes.punchline: His summary of the elaborate betrayal is 'my friends totally boned me' — said to a priest, with complete sincerity, while also being literally accurate about what friendship with these people means
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — 'boned' in a confessional is a slight tonal collision but not particularly fresh. Gets a minor chuckle. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: Priest: 'If I smite your friends and absolve you, will you leave?' / Mac: 'Yeah.' / Priest: 'You're absolved, and your friends are smited.'
jokes.setup: The priest has completely given up on the actual sacrament
jokes.punchline: The priest offers to fake-perform both absolution AND divine smiting as a transaction to get Mac to leave — entirely abandoning his religious role for practical escape purposes
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff to the opening smite request. The priest's complete capitulation — offering to 'smite' Mac's friends in exchange for Mac leaving — is funny because it confirms the priest has abandoned all pretense of religious authenticity in favor of getting this madman out of his booth. 'Your friends are smited' is delivered with the same priestly formality as an actual sacrament. Strong economy and structure.

jokes.text: Priest: 'In the name of the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Please leave.'
jokes.setup: The priest has just agreed to perform fake absolution and smiting
jokes.punchline: He appends 'Please leave' directly to the liturgical formula — combining the sacred closing of the sacrament with a desperate personal request — delivered in the same priestly register
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the two-word addition 'Please leave' appended to a sacred formula is a masterclass in brevity. The joke is entirely in the juxtaposition: solemn liturgy + exhausted human desperation in one breath. No wasted words, big laugh. One of the tightest jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Oh, um, when should I see the results?' / Priest: 'What are you talking about?' / Mac: 'When does the spell kick in? When is God gonna shed some of this weight for me?'
jokes.setup: Mac has been absolved and told to leave
jokes.punchline: Mac treats the absolution as a magic spell for weight loss — 'when does the spell kick in?' — and expects God to personally remove his weight as a consequence of the transaction
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing character joke. Mac's transactional relationship with God is the entire thesis of his character. He genuinely believes confession + absolution = divine weight-loss service, delivered as a customer asking about shipment timing. 'When does the spell kick in?' is a great line. Connects back to the opening 'I'm fat' confession elegantly.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Not hard. Perfect.' — satisfied customer, leaving God a 5-star review
jokes.setup: Priest says six weeks for God's weight-loss spell
jokes.punchline: Mac's response is the casual satisfaction of someone who got the answer they wanted from customer support — 'Not hard. Perfect.' — as though he's confirming a convenient delivery window
jokes.explanation: Four syllables doing enormous work. 'Not hard. Perfect.' in response to 'God will fix your weight in six weeks' is the ideal button — it confirms Mac's transactional, consumer-service relationship with the divine. The casualness is everything. Perfect economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Mac's closing prayer: 'Uh, glory unto you, ghost man in the sky that created us all and predetermines everything. I'll see you in six weeks.'
jokes.setup: Mac wraps up his confessional visit
jokes.punchline: His improvised prayer addresses God as 'ghost man in the sky' and includes 'predetermines everything' (a theological position undermining confession itself) and closes with 'I'll see you in six weeks' as a casual appointment confirmation
jokes.explanation: A magnificent closing joke. 'Ghost man in the sky' as Mac's conception of God is both reverent (he means it) and deflating. 'Predetermines everything' inadvertently makes confession pointless. 'I'll see you in six weeks' — treating God like a personal trainer appointment — is the perfect final note. The entire episode's theological framework gets dismantled in one improvised prayer. High character integration, high quotability, great episode closer.

tmdb_overview: Step inside the confession booth with Mac as he tells a befuddled priest why his fatness is the fault of the other members of The Gang.
